summary: Varun Pant opens by motivating formal verification in the age of coding agents: with builders producing hundreds or thousands of pull requests weekly, probabilistic LM judging, finite tests, and non-scaling human review cannot prove correctness for every input. Formal verification provides a mathematical proof that code satisfies a specification for all inputs. He describes a workflow in which humans own the specification (either written in Lean or auto-formalized from natural language) and validate it before downstream work, while machines own the implementation and the proof. Lean serves as both programming language and proof assistant, eliminating a translation layer, and features a small trusted kernel whose proofs can be exported and independently re-checked. He likens interactive proof to chess: tactics are moves toward a checkmating theorem, with backtracking when a branch fails. A concrete demonstration shows an AI spending roughly a week converting zlib into Lean, decompressing into lemmas, applying tactics, and assembling 32,000 lines of proof verified by the kernel. For code that cannot move to Lean, the Cedar authorization system keeps its functional semantics in Lean while the production runtime is Rust, reconciled nightly by approximately 100 million differential random tests; no version ships until they agree. Solvers (e.g., Z3) act as calculators, with pre/post conditions enforced statically and erased at runtime. Finally, AWS's open-source Strata tool lowers any language into a shared Strata core written in Lean, which can dispatch to Lean provers, SMT solvers, or model checkers.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Why none of the usual checks clear agent output
sections.summary: Coding agents produce hundreds to thousands of PRs weekly; LM-as-judge is probabilistic, tests cover only some inputs, and human review does not scale. Formal verification is introduced as a way to prove correctness for all inputs.

sections.title: Specifications humans own, proofs machines own
sections.summary: Humans own the specification (written in Lean or auto-formalized from natural language) and must validate it upstream; machines own the code and the proof. The validated spec is the live artifact the builder interacts with, and everything else is downstream.

sections.title: Lean as one language for code and proof
sections.summary: Lean combines programming and proof assistance in one language with no translation layer, is implemented in itself, and has a small trusted kernel whose proofs can be exported and independently checked. A list-reverse example shows code and a theorem in the same file.

sections.title: Tactics, theorems, and the chess analogy
sections.summary: Tactics are like chess moves toward a checkmating theorem, with backtracking when a goal will not close; the small kernel confirms the result. Multiple independent kernels in C++, Rust, and Lean exist because the system is open source.

sections.title: Rewriting zlib into Lean, and 32,000 lines of proof
sections.summary: An AI took about a week to convert zlib from C to Lean, writing a natural-language spec, having the AI auto-formalize it, generating the Lean code, and producing helper lemma subgoals that are proved with tactics and assembled into a final theorem verified by the kernel, totaling 32,000 lines of proof.

sections.title: Cedar: Lean semantics, Rust in production
sections.summary: Cedar's functional specification lives in Lean while production code runs in Rust; they are reconciled by about 100 million nightly differential random tests, and no version ships until they agree. An example 'forbid permits' policy illustrates the property that every satisfied forbid policy denies the request.

sections.title: Solvers, preconditions, and code erased at runtime
sections.summary: A solver like Z3 is a calculator returning satisfiable or unsatisfiable. Verus embeds requires/ensures pre- and post-conditions inline, enforced statically and erased at runtime like ghost code. Eneus translates Rust's MIR to Lean and reuses the same interactive theorem prover.

sections.title: Bringing any language into the same core
sections.summary: AWS's open-source Strata tool lets users define a dialect for any language, lowering it through a high-level IR to the Lean-based Strata core, which can dispatch to the Lean prover, SMT solvers, or model checkers. The talk closes by inviting viewers to try Lean in the browser on their most critical code.

demonstrations: Lean file with a list-reverse function and an in-language theorem proving reverse(a ++ b) = reverse b ++ reverse a.
Incorrect Lean proof being rejected immediately by the kernel.
AI re-implementing zlib in Lean over about a week, decomposing into lemmas, proving each, and assembling 32,000 lines of proof verified by the kernel.
Cedar example showing Rust production code checked against a Lean functional specification via nightly differential random testing.
Verus snippet illustrating requires/ensures pre- and post-conditions enforced statically and erased at runtime.
limitations: Specification correctness is critical because everything else is downstream from it.
The agent was granted about a week to rewrite zlib in Lean.
Strata is described as work in progress.
LM-as-judge, tests, and human review do not scale or cover all inputs.

organization.name: AWS
organization.summary: Amazon Web Services (AWS) is Amazon's cloud subsidiary and the world's most comprehensive cloud platform. First-party pages describe a global infrastructure with 240+ services, including AI capabilities used by millions of customers. AWS Automated Reasoning teams publish Cedar, an open-source authorization policy language whose Lean formal model is differentially tested against the Rust production runtime, and are building Strata, an open-source Lean-based intermediate representation for verifying any language. Varun Pant builds AI products at AWS leading formal-verification work and presents Cedar and Strata in this talk. Lean is the proof assistant used, not the featured organization.
organization.status: Amazon subsidiary as of the research date. aws.amazon.com, the Amazon about-AWS page, and the AWS Open Source blog post on Lean-verified Cedar are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
